text: Heart failure sounds like the heart has stopped. But it hasn't. It's still beating, every second. So what is failing? And why do people with heart failure get breathless and swollen? Let's find out.

Heart failure means the heart can't pump enough blood to meet the body's needs. The muscle is too weak to squeeze well, or too stiff to fill well. Either way, blood moves forward too slowly, and fluid starts to back up.

What causes it? Most often, damage from a heart attack, or years of high blood pressure. Other causes include leaky or narrow valves, diseases of the heart muscle, diabetes, and long-term heavy alcohol use.

Doctors measure how much blood the left ventricle pumps out with each beat. This is the ejection fraction. In a healthy heart, it's about fifty to seventy percent. At forty percent or lower, the heart is pumping weakly.

When the left side fails, blood backs up into the lungs. Fluid leaks into the air sacs, so breathing gets hard, especially when lying flat. Some people wake up at night gasping, or need extra pillows to sleep.
When the right side fails, blood backs up into the veins of the body. Fluid collects in the legs and ankles, and sometimes in the belly. Press on a swollen ankle, and a dent stays behind.

So the main signs are shortness of breath, tiredness, swollen feet and ankles, and quick weight gain from fluid. If breathing suddenly becomes very hard, or there is chest pain or fainting, call your local emergency number.
To find it, doctors listen to the heart and lungs, take a chest x-ray, check a blood test called B N P, and use an ultrasound of the heart, called an echocardiogram, to see how well it pumps.

Heart failure usually can't be cured, but it can be controlled. Medicines help the heart work better and water pills remove extra fluid. Eat less salt, weigh yourself every day, stay active as advised, and treat the cause.

So remember three things. Heart failure means a weak or stiff pump, not a stopped heart. Left side failure floods the lungs, right side failure swells the legs. And with treatment, many people live well for years. Next, we'll see what happens when the heart's rhythm goes wrong.
